name: POPE: Polling-based Object Probing Evaluation for Object Hallucination in Large Vision-Language Models
description: POPE (Polling-based Object Probing Evaluation) is a benchmark dataset and evaluation framework for assessing object hallucination in Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs). It converts hallucination evaluation into a binary classification task by prompting LVLMs with Yes/No questions about objects in images. The dataset is built on MSCOCO, A-OKVQA, and GQA, using three sampling strategies (Random, Popular, Adversarial) to construct polling questions about ground-truth and nonexistent objects. The study also evaluates hallucination using the CHAIR metric on MSCOCO across multiple LVLMs including mPLUG-Owl, LLaVA, MultiModal-GPT, MiniGPT-4, and InstructBLIP.
creator: Yifan Li, Yifan Du, Kun Zhou, Jinpeng Wang, Wayne Xin Zhao, Ji-Rong Wen (Renmin University of China, Meituan Group)
citeAs: Yifan Li, Yifan Du, Kun Zhou, Jinpeng Wang, Wayne Xin Zhao, Ji-Rong Wen. Evaluating Object Hallucination in Large Vision-Language Models. arXiv:2305.10355v3 [cs.CV], 26 Oct 2023.
rai:dataCollection: The evaluation dataset is constructed from the validation set of MSCOCO, randomly sampling 500 images with more than 3 ground-truth objects for POPE evaluation, and 2,000 images with annotations for CHAIR metric evaluation. POPE is also extended to A-OKVQA and GQA datasets using automatic segmentation with SEEM. Ground-truth objects are obtained either from human annotations or automatic segmentation tools (SEEM). Polling questions are constructed with a 1:1 ratio of ground-truth to nonexistent objects for label balance, with 6 questions per image.
rai:dataCollectionRawData: Images and object annotations from MSCOCO validation set (Lin et al., 2014), A-OKVQA (Schwenk et al., 2022), and GQA (Hudson and Manning, 2019). For CHAIR evaluation, 2,000 images are randomly sampled from the MSCOCO validation set. For POPE, 500 images with more than 3 ground-truth objects are randomly selected from MSCOCO validation set.
rai:dataManipulationProtocol: Three negative object sampling strategies are used to construct nonexistent object questions: (1) Random Sampling: randomly sample objects not present in the image; (2) Popular Sampling: select the top-k most frequent objects in the whole dataset that do not exist in the current image; (3) Adversarial Sampling: rank objects by co-occurrence frequency with ground-truth objects and select top-k frequent ones not present in the image. The ratio between ground-truth and nonexistent objects is set to 1:1 for label balance.
rai:dataPreprocessingProtocol: For CHAIR evaluation, only 80 objects appearing in the MSCOCO segmentation challenge are considered, following Rohrbach et al. (2018). For POPE, images with more than 3 ground-truth objects are selected. For SEEM-based POPE, the SEEM segmentation tool is used to automatically annotate objects in unannotated datasets. ChatGPT is used to parse open-ended LVLM responses for VQA evaluation.
rai:dataAnnotationProtocol: Ground-truth object annotations are taken from existing human-labeled MSCOCO annotations. For unannotated datasets (A-OKVQA, GQA), automatic segmentation using SEEM (Segment Everything Everywhere All at Once) is used to obtain object labels. Polling questions are formulated using the template 'Is there a/an <object> in the image?' with binary Yes/No answers.
rai:dataAnnotationPlatform: SEEM (Segment Everything Everywhere All at Once) for automatic segmentation-based annotation; MSCOCO human annotations for ground-truth objects.
rai:dataAnnotationAnalysis: The consistency between POPE Yes/No responses and model-generated captions was validated. Out of 1303 and 1445 objects given 'No' responses by InstructBLIP and MiniGPT-4 respectively, merely 0 and 5 of those objects were referenced in captions. Out of 664 and 1034 objects mentioned in captions, 664 and 961 respectively received a 'Yes' verdict, confirming robust correlation. Performance gap between annotation-based and SEEM-based POPE was noted (e.g., F1 Score 71.37 vs. 62.70 for MiniGPT-4 under Adversarial setting), attributed to finer granularity of SEEM segmentation results.
rai:annotationsPerItem: 6 questions per image (3 ground-truth object questions with 'Yes' answers and 3 nonexistent object questions with 'No' answers, maintaining a 1:1 ratio)
rai:machineAnnotationTools: SEEM (Segment Everything Everywhere All at Once, Zou et al., 2023) for automatic object segmentation and annotation; ChatGPT for parsing open-ended LVLM responses in VQA evaluation.
rai:dataSocialImpact: Object hallucination in LVLMs can lead to unexpected consequences in real-world applications. For example, in autonomous driving systems, incorrect understanding of the external environment due to hallucinated objects could cause wrong decisions when encountering unexpected events, potentially leading to serious safety issues. The work also highlights risks for blind users relying on AI-generated image captions.
rai:dataBiases: Visual instruction datasets used to train LVLMs (mostly based on MSCOCO) have an unbalanced object distribution where top frequent objects occupy a major part of the dataset. This causes LVLMs to be prone to hallucinate frequently appearing objects and objects that frequently co-occur with image objects. Approximately half of hallucinated objects in each image belong to the top 10 frequently appearing COCO objects, and more than half are among the top 10 frequently co-occurring objects. LVLMs like LLaVA, MultiModal-GPT, and mPLUG-Owl are extremely prone to answer 'Yes' (near 99%), indicating overconfidence bias.
rai:dataLimitations: The evaluation focuses only on coarse-grained object hallucinations (object presence), not fine-grained aspects such as object number, attributes, or positions. Due to computational resource limitations, models are evaluated on a subset of the validation set, which may be affected by data distribution. POPE uses a matching-based method to determine Yes/No answers, but LVLMs may occasionally fail to provide explicit Yes/No answers, leading to inaccurate evaluation. When using automatic segmentation tools, objects are annotated based on the tool's label set, which may be inconsistent with human annotations. Only a small number of LVLMs are compared, excluding recently released or closed-source models. The degree of hallucination may not always be consistent with VQA performance.
rai:dataUseCases: Testing and evaluation of object hallucination in Large Vision-Language Models (LVLMs). The POPE benchmark can be used to evaluate hallucination stability across different prompt templates, assess hallucination severity under Random, Popular, and Adversarial sampling settings, extend evaluation to unannotated datasets using automatic segmentation tools, and correlate hallucination performance with VQA and image captioning performance.
